guide.title: Monti, Rome: The North Half of the Imperial Fora, Four Towers and the Lateran
guide.intro: Monti is rione I in Roma Capitale's list of Rome's 22 rioni, toponymic code 101. The Comune says the rione was named for three of the seven hills — the Esquiline, the Viminal and part of the Quirinal — and that the Esquiline no longer forms part of it. Half of the Imperial Fora stand here. Via dei Fori Imperiali is the boundary with Campitelli, and the Forum of Trajan, Trajan's Column, the Markets of Trajan and the Forum of Augustus are all on the Monti side of the road. Above them rise four medieval towers, one of them built by a pope for his brother. Roma Capitale also names the cathedral of Rome, San Giovanni in Laterano, among the monuments present in the rione, and Santa Maria Maggiore stands on a seam the Comune's own pages do not resolve.

sections.heading: The Imperial Fora, north of the road
sections.body:
Via dei Fori Imperiali, opened in 1932 as via dell'Impero, runs between Monti and Campitelli, and the archaeological strip it crosses is cut in two by it. The Forum of Trajan, Trajan's Column, the Markets of Trajan with the Museo dei Fori Imperiali, and the Forum of Augustus with the Arco dei Pantani and the Aula del Colosso are all on the Monti side. The fora on the south side belong to Campitelli, and so does the ticketed walkway that crosses beneath the road: it enters at the Trajan's Column end, in Monti, and leaves at the Foro di Cesare on via Bonella, in Campitelli.

Roma Capitale dates Trajan's Column to 113 AD and credits the design to Apollodorus of Damascus: about forty metres with the base, seventeen monolithic drums, an internal spiral stair of 185 steps, and Trajan's ashes in the base — he died on 8 August 117. In 1587 Sixtus V put a figure of St Peter on top of it in place of the lost bronze statue. Behind the Forum of Augustus stands a firewall of peperino, pietra gabina and travertine, up to thirty-three metres high, built to shield the forum from the fires of the Suburra: the crowded low quarter that the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione places around the Argiletum, on the line of today's via Leonina and via Madonna dei Monti.

Uphill from the fora are the towers. The Torre delle Milizie, about fifty metres, is entered today through the Markets of Trajan; the Torre dei Capocci is thirty-six metres of brick on piazza di San Martino ai Monti; the Torre del Grillo carries the corner eagles and the inscription EX MARCHIONE DE GRILLIS that the del Grillo family added after buying it in 1675; and the Torre dei Conti, on largo Corrado Ricci, was built around 1203 by Pope Innocent III for his brother Riccardo and has one of the four squared-tufa exedrae of the Forum of Peace in its cellars.

sections.heading: The Lateran, Santa Maria Maggiore and the seams
sections.body:
Roma Capitale's own page for Rione I – Monti names the Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano among the monuments, archaeological sites and places of worship present in the rione, describing it as the cathedral of Rome. The Comune's perimeter description for the rione lists «complesso del Laterano (entro le mura aureliane)» among the rione's boundary elements. The complex is not indivisible, though: boundary tests put the Scala Santa on the Esquilino side, and it is not covered in this guide. What is covered is the basilica, the baptistery, the Palazzo del Laterano where the Lateran Pacts were signed on 11 February 1929, the Lateran obelisk and the treasury museum.

Three of those properties belong to a legal tier that is neither Italian in the ordinary way nor Vatican. Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of them (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that such a property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. They are on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. That is worth reading twice, because one of the museums inside the Palazzo del Laterano is called the Museo storico vaticano and stands on Italian soil, not in Vatican City.

Santa Maria Maggiore is the unresolved case. Roma Capitale's material on the basilica is internally inconsistent. Its Rione I – Monti page names the basilica among the monuments present in the rione; the same page states that the Esquiline hill no longer forms part of the rione, and its page for the basilica places the basilica on the summit of the Esquiline hill. The rione assignment is unresolved. The postcodes change across the block too — 00184 on the facade side, 00185 at Piazza di Santa Maria Maggiore 28.

Several of the streets a visitor will walk are the rione's edges rather than its interior. Roma Capitale's perimeter for Monti reads: «piazza del Colosseo, via dei Fori Imperiali, piazza Madonna di Loreto, vicolo San Bernardo, via Magnanapoli, via XXIV Maggio, via del Quirinale, via delle Quattro Fontane, via Agostino Depretis, piazza Esquilino; via Esquilino, piazza Santa Maria Maggiore, via Merulana, piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, complesso del Laterano (entro le mura aureliane), via della Ferratella, piazza di Porta Metronia, via della Navicella, via Santo Stefano Rotondo, via Oliviero Plunkett, via di San Giovanni in Laterano.» Via Merulana and via del Quirinale are boundaries, not interior streets, and this guide claims neither piazza del Quirinale nor piazza del Colosseo for Monti.

The interior streets are where the rione's own names survive. The Italian Wikipedia article on the rione records that via in Selci follows the ancient Vicus Suburranus and takes its name from the paving stones found during works there; that the salita dei Borgia runs partly along what is believed to be the Vicus sceleratus; that vicolo delle Carrette survives from a piazza and street where the carts bringing wine and food from the Castelli waited by the Forum market; that via Magnanapoli is said to be a corruption of Balnea Napoli; and that via degli Annibaldi and its neighbours are named for the families who held fortified houses and towers there. An inscription in piazza della Suburra still records the edicola di San Salvatore delle tre immagini ai Monti.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The metro station inside Monti is Cavour, at Via Cavour 197, 00184. The Italian Wikipedia article on the rione says Line B serves it. Colosseo station is contested between Monti and Celio and is not claimed here, and no source was obtained for which lines other than B serve it, so none is named.

Via Cavour itself was opened at the end of the nineteenth century to link the Esquiline to piazza Venezia through the Suburra valley, per the same article. Via Nazionale was «istituita il 30 novembre 1871», originally joining piazza Venezia to piazza dell'Esedra, which was renamed piazza della Repubblica in 1953; Palazzo delle Esposizioni is at Via Nazionale 194, 00184, and the Banca d'Italia head office at Palazzo Koch is at Via Nazionale 91, 00184.

Other street addresses worth writing down: San Pietro in Vincoli at Piazza di San Pietro in Vincoli 4/a, 00184; San Clemente at Via Labicana 95, 00184, which Roma Capitale places «circa 300 metri oltre il Colosseo», about 300 metres beyond the Colosseum; the Markets of Trajan at Via Quattro Novembre 94, 00187; Sant'Andrea al Quirinale at Via del Quirinale 30, 00187; the Museo Vite di IMI at Via Labicana 15a, 00184; Mercato Monti at Via Leonina 46/48, 00184; and Ai Tre Scalini at Via Panisperna 249/251, 00184.

One warning about hours. Only one place in this guide publishes them: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, Tuesday to Sunday 9.00–12.00 and 15.00–18.00, closed Monday, from the church's own site. No source states hours for Santa Maria Maggiore or the Domus Aurea, so neither carries opening or ticketing information here. Check before you travel.

faq.question: Is the Colosseum in Monti?
faq.answer: No. Roma Capitale's page for Rione I – Monti names fourteen monuments as present in the rione and the Colosseum is not among them; the amphitheatre and piazza del Colosseo are in the neighbouring rione of Celio. The Comune does name piazza del Colosseo in the rione's perimeter — as a boundary element, not as something inside it. The Colosseum is not covered in this guide. It appears here only where a source names it: Roma Capitale says Nero's artificial lake at the Domus Aurea lay in the valley where the Colosseum was later built, and it places San Clemente about 300 metres beyond it.

faq.question: Which rione is Santa Maria Maggiore in?
faq.answer: Roma Capitale's material on Santa Maria Maggiore is internally inconsistent. Its Rione I – Monti page names the basilica among the monuments present in the rione; the same page states that the Esquiline hill no longer forms part of the rione, and its page for the basilica places the basilica on the summit of the Esquiline hill. The rione assignment is unresolved. The postcodes seam across the block as well, 00184 on the facade side and 00185 at Piazza di Santa Maria Maggiore 28. The basilica is written up here once, under Monti, with the seam stated rather than smoothed over.

faq.question: Are the Lateran buildings and Santa Maria Maggiore part of Vatican City?
faq.answer: No. They are a third legal tier. Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of these properties (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. The Museo storico vaticano, whose name suggests otherwise, stands inside the Palazzo del Laterano on Italian soil.

faq.question: Where does Monti begin and end?
faq.answer: Roma Capitale publishes a perimeter for the rione in words: «piazza del Colosseo, via dei Fori Imperiali, piazza Madonna di Loreto, vicolo San Bernardo, via Magnanapoli, via XXIV Maggio, via del Quirinale, via delle Quattro Fontane, via Agostino Depretis, piazza Esquilino; via Esquilino, piazza Santa Maria Maggiore, via Merulana, piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, complesso del Laterano (entro le mura aureliane), via della Ferratella, piazza di Porta Metronia, via della Navicella, via Santo Stefano Rotondo, via Oliviero Plunkett, via di San Giovanni in Laterano.» Those streets are the edges. Via Merulana, via del Quirinale and via dei Fori Imperiali are all boundaries rather than interior streets.

faq.question: How do I reach Monti on the metro?
faq.answer: Cavour station, at Via Cavour 197, 00184, is inside the rione, and the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione says Line B serves it. Colosseo station is contested between Monti and Celio, so this guide does not claim it, and no transit-authority source was obtained for the other lines said to call there.

faq.question: Which places in this guide publish opening hours?
faq.answer: One. Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, Via del Quirinale 30, 00187, gives its hours on its own website: Tuesday to Sunday 9.00–12.00 and 15.00–18.00, closed Monday. Nothing else here carries hours, tickets or opening information, because no source states them — including Santa Maria Maggiore and the Domus Aurea. Treat every other entry as a description of what a place is and where it stands, not a statement that it is open today.

photos.title: Colonna Traiana
photos.description: Trajan's Column in the Forum of Trajan, on the Monti side of via dei Fori Imperiali, erected in 113 AD and carrying a spiral relief up seventeen monolithic marble drums.
photos.author: Alvesgaspar

places.name: Mercati di Traiano — Museo dei Fori Imperiali
places.summary: Six levels of Roman building stepped up the slope of the Quirinal alongside the Forum of Trajan, now holding the Museo dei Fori Imperiali. The markets and the museum are one institution, not two.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the complex was given the name Mercati di Traiano at its rediscovery of 1926–1934. Conservation and structural restoration ran from 2005 to 2007, and the Museo dei Fori Imperiali was inaugurated in the autumn of 2007. The Torre delle Milizie is entered through it. One caution about the address: the street entrance is on via Quattro Novembre, which boundary tests place on the Trevi side of the line, so no rione is claimed here for the doorway itself.

places.name: Colonna Traiana
places.summary: The column erected in 113 AD, about forty metres tall with its base, devised by the architect Apollodorus of Damascus.
places.history: Roma Capitale records seventeen monolithic drums and an internal spiral stair of 185 steps. Trajan's ashes were placed in the base; he died on 8 August 117. In 1587 Sixtus V replaced the lost bronze statue at the top with a figure of St Peter.

places.name: Foro di Traiano
places.summary: One of the Imperial Fora, on the north side of via dei Fori Imperiali and so on the Monti side of the boundary with Campitelli. The Basilica Ulpia is a component of this forum rather than a separate site.
places.history: Roma Capitale publishes a dating table for the Imperial Fora on its area-archeologica-dei-fori-imperiali page. That table was not obtained during verification, so no construction date is given here.

places.name: Foro di Augusto
places.summary: The forum inaugurated in 2 BC around the temple of Mars Ultor, on the Monti side of via dei Fori Imperiali.
places.history: Roma Capitale describes the temple in white Carrara marble, eight columns across the front and seven along each side, of which three still stand on the south-east side. Behind it rises a firewall of peperino, pietra gabina and travertine, up to thirty-three metres high, raised to shield the forum from the fires of the Suburra. The second opening through that wall is the Arco dei Pantani, a single travertine span. The Aula del Colosso, which the Comune names on its Imperial Fora page, housed the colossal Genius of Augustus, whose remains are now in the Museo dei Fori Imperiali. The Comune's page also records that in the Middle Ages the podium of the temple was occupied by the church of San Basilio, «ora scomparsa» — now vanished.

places.name: Domus Aurea
places.summary: Nero's palace complex, begun after the fire of 64 AD.
places.history: Roma Capitale names the architects Severus and Celer and the decorator Fabullus, also given as Famulus. The complex held pavilions, gardens and an artificial lake in the valley where the Colosseum was later built, and included the octagonal hall known as the coenatio rotunda. No source states its opening or ticketing information, so none is given here.

places.name: Terme di Traiano
places.summary: A bath complex on the Colle Oppio designed by Apollodorus of Damascus and dedicated by Trajan in 109 AD, covering over six hectares.
places.history: It overlies the Esquiline wing of the Domus Aurea and the Terme di Tito. Roma Capitale says the plan has been reconstructed from remains found during the creation of the Parco Traiano in the 1930s, from fragments of the Forma Urbis Severiana, and from sixteenth- and seventeenth-century drawings.

places.name: Terme di Tito
places.summary: A bath building dedicated in 80 AD, on the south slope of the Colle Oppio.
places.history: Little of it survives. Roma Capitale records that Andrea Palladio drew the baths when they were still visible in the 1500s.

places.name: Ludus Magnus
places.summary: A gladiatorial training school on via Labicana.
places.history: Roma Capitale names the Ludus Magnus among the monuments, archaeological sites and places of worship present in Rione Monti.

places.name: Suburra
places.summary: The ancient quarter that gave this part of Rome its character, and the reason the Forum of Augustus has a thirty-three-metre firewall behind it.
places.history: The Italian Wikipedia article on the rione describes the Suburra in Roman times as the low, marshy ground around the Argiletum, on the line of today's via Leonina and via Madonna dei Monti, drained by the Cloaca Massima; its upper part ran towards the Vicus Patricius, today via Urbana. Roma Capitale's own page for the Forum of Augustus explains the great wall behind that forum as a shield against the fires of the Suburra — the Comune's explanation, not the encyclopaedia's. The same Wikipedia article records that an inscription in piazza della Suburra still names the edicola di San Salvatore delle tre immagini ai Monti, a street shrine that no longer stands.

places.name: Parco del Colle Oppio
places.summary: The public park on the Colle Oppio, the hill that carries the Terme di Traiano above the Esquiline wing of the Domus Aurea.
places.history: Roma Capitale dates the works that created the Parco Traiano, on the same hill, to the 1930s, and says the reconstructed plan of the Terme di Traiano rests partly on remains found during them.

places.name: Torre delle Milizie
places.summary: A brick tower of about fifty metres, reached from the Salita del Grillo and entered today through the Mercati di Traiano.
places.history: Roma Capitale dates its construction «con ogni probabilità agli inizi del XIII secolo» — in all probability to the beginning of the thirteenth century — and attributes it to the Conti di Segni. It passed to the Annibaldi, the Prefetti di Vico and Boniface VIII Caetani, then back to the Conti until the 1600s, and was absorbed into the monastery of Santa Caterina a Magnanapoli before being isolated after 1910. An earthquake in the mid-fourteenth century brought down the third storey and started the lean. Two arms of Roma Capitale publish different years for that earthquake, so no year is given here.

places.name: Torre del Grillo
places.summary: A tower also called «della Miliziola», built in 1223 by the Carboni family on Trajanic remains and later absorbed into the left wing of the Palazzo del Grillo.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the del Grillo family bought it in 1675 and added the corbelled crown, the corner eagles and the inscription EX MARCHIONE DE GRILLIS. It passed to the Nicolis de Robilant in the 1800s. After the Second World War it housed Renato Guttuso's studio, and its hanging garden lies behind his La visita della sera of 1980 and Giardino di Palazzo del Grillo of 1981.

places.name: Torre dei Capocci
places.address: Piazza di San Martino ai Monti 16, Roma RM
places.summary: A square brick tower of thirty-six metres on piazza di San Martino ai Monti, seven floors above a ground floor and a terrace.
places.history: Roma Capitale says it was built by the Arcioni and later held by the Capocci. The upper brick section is original and dates to the late twelfth century, its brick taken from the Terme di Traiano. The houses around it were demolished at the end of the nineteenth century, which is why the colour of the masonry changes at third-floor level. The Comune describes the tower as «di proprietà del Comune di Roma, attualmente non visitabile all'interno» — owned by the Comune di Roma and not at present visitable inside.

places.name: Torre dei Conti
places.summary: A medieval tower on largo Corrado Ricci, at the edge of the Imperial Fora.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that the Torre dei Conti was built by Pope Innocent III Conti (1198–1216) around 1203 for his brother Riccardo, as a fortified residence for himself and his family. It stood about 60 metres high. After earthquake damage and further collapses in the seventeenth century it was reduced to its present height and turned into a timber store and hayloft. Its cellars incorporate one of the four squared-tufa exedrae of the Forum of Peace (71–75 AD).

places.name: Casa dei Cavalieri di Rodi
places.summary: A house on piazza del Grillo. Roma Capitale names the Casa dei Cavalieri di Rodi among the monuments, archaeological sites and places of worship present in Rione Monti.
places.history: No per-place page for it was found on turismoroma, museiincomuneroma or sovraintendenzaroma, and the street number here comes from OpenStreetMap. This record therefore carries the name, the address and the Comune's mention, and nothing further.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore
places.address: Piazza di Santa Maria Maggiore, Roma RM
places.summary: One of the four papal basilicas of Rome, per Roma Capitale. Its block sits on the seam between Monti and Esquilino: the postcode is 00184 on the facade side and 00185 at Piazza di Santa Maria Maggiore 28.
places.history:
Roma Capitale's material on Santa Maria Maggiore is internally inconsistent. Its Rione I – Monti page names the basilica among the monuments present in the rione; the same page states that the Esquiline hill no longer forms part of the rione, and its page for the basilica places the basilica on the summit of the Esquiline hill. The rione assignment is unresolved. The basilica is written up once, here, rather than in two rioni.

Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. Art. 13 names the basilica explicitly, and Annex II, Tav. 2 names the «Basilica di S. Maria Maggiore con gli edifici annessi».

Roma Capitale records the commemoration of the snow miracle on 5 August; the two great chapels, the Sistina and the Paolina, raised by Sixtus V and Paul V between the late sixteenth and the early seventeenth century; and nave mosaics of the fifth century.

No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

places.name: Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano
places.address: Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: Roma Capitale's own page for Rione I – Monti names the Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano among the monuments, archaeological sites and places of worship present in the rione, describing it as the cathedral of Rome. The Comune's perimeter description for the rione lists «complesso del Laterano (entro le mura aureliane)» among the rione's boundary elements.
places.history:
Roma Capitale's phrase for it is «la cattedrale di Roma, madre di tutte le chiese di Roma e del mondo». The basilica's own site carries the motto Mater et Caput Omnium Ecclesiarum.

Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. Art. 13 names the basilica explicitly, and Annex II, Tav. 1 names the «Basilica e Palazzo Apostolico Lateranense ed annessi con la Scala Santa».

The complex around it is not a single unit for the purposes of this corpus: the Scala Santa is in the rione Esquilino, and is written up there rather than here.

places.name: Battistero lateranense
places.address: Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: The baptistery beside the basilica, built in the fourth century by Constantine over a first-century villa and a second-century bath building. Its plan is octagonal, on eight porphyry columns with Corinthian capitals.
places.history:
The external frieze of 1657, with the Chigi arms, is by Francesco Borromini. The old portico was converted in 1054 into the chapels of Rufina and Seconda and of Cipriano and Giustina, the second of which keeps a fifth-century mosaic.

High on the walls are modern copies of works by Andrea Sacchi showing scenes from the life of John the Baptist; below them, frescoes of scenes from the life of Constantine by Andrea Camassei, Giacinto Gimignani and Carlo Maratta. At the centre of a sixteenth-century circular enclosure stands the font, an urn of green basalt with a bronze cover by Ciro Ferri (1634–1689). Two bronze deer were placed there in 1967 by Pope Paul VI.

places.name: Palazzo del Laterano
places.address: Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, Roma RM
places.summary: The palace in which the Lateran Pacts were signed on 11 February 1929. The Italian Wikipedia article on the Pacts says they «presero il nome del Palazzo di San Giovanni in Laterano in cui furono firmati» — took their name from the palace in which they were signed. The signature date is corroborated by the treaty text published by the Holy See.
places.history:
Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership of this property (Art. 13; Annex II). Art. 15 states that the property, «benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano» — although forming part of the territory of the Italian State — enjoys the immunities that international law grants to the headquarters of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. It is on Italian soil and visitors are subject to Italian law. Annex II, Tav. 1 names the «Basilica e Palazzo Apostolico Lateranense ed annessi con la Scala Santa», which is where the palace's status comes from.

One name inside the building misleads: the Museo storico vaticano stands in the Palazzo del Laterano, on Italian soil. It is not in Vatican City. it is.

places.name: Obelisco Lateranense
places.address: Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, Roma RM
places.summary: An obelisk of red Aswan granite on piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano: 32.18 metres of shaft, 45.70 metres with its cross and base, and 455 tonnes.
places.history: Roma Capitale places its making under Thutmose III and Thutmose IV, in the fifteenth century BC. Constantine had it brought down the Nile to Alexandria; the transport was interrupted by his death in 337.

places.name: Museo del Tesoro Lateranense
places.address: Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: The treasury museum of the Lateran basilica, which carries its own pages on the basilica's website. It also appears under the name Museo di San Giovanni in Laterano; the two names belong to one museum, not two.
places.history: No source states more than the name, the identification and the address.

places.name: Museo storico vaticano
places.address: Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A museum inside the Palazzo del Laterano. Its name misleads: it stands on Italian soil, not in Vatican City.
places.history: No source states more than the name, the location inside the Palazzo del Laterano and the address.

places.name: Obelisco Esquilino
places.summary: An obelisk of red Aswan granite standing in piazza dell'Esquilino, behind the apse of Santa Maria Maggiore: 14.75 metres, or 25.53 metres with its base. Roma Capitale's page for it places the obelisk «nel Rione Monti», in the Comune's own words.
places.history: The shaft carries no inscription, which prevents it from being dated; Roma Capitale considers it probably of Roman manufacture. Latin inscriptions are carved on each side of the base. It was raised here in 1587 under Sixtus V to a design by Domenico Fontana, who worked with his brother Marsilio and his nephew Carlo Maderno.

places.name: Basilica di San Pietro in Vincoli
places.address: Piazza di San Pietro in Vincoli 4/a, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A church on its own piazza in Monti.
places.history: OpenStreetMap records Michelangelo's Moses at this church. No source from Roma Capitale or from the parish states more.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria ai Monti
places.address: Via Madonna dei Monti, Roma RM
places.summary: A church built from 1580 by Giacomo Della Porta for Gregory XIII, on the site of a thirteenth-century Clarissan monastery.
places.history: Roma Capitale says the church was raised after a blind woman's cure was attributed to an icon found on the site. Della Porta modelled the facade on that of the Gesù, which he also built. Inside, on a single nave, the vault Ascensione is by Cristoforo Casolani, of the early seventeenth century; the stucco angels of 1588 are by Ambrogio Buonvicino; and the high altar carries a Virgin and Child with SS Stephen and Lawrence of the early fifteenth century.

places.name: Basilica di San Clemente al Laterano
places.summary: Two superimposed churches standing over Republican-era Roman buildings and a Mithraeum. Roma Capitale says the first church was «eretta prima del 385» — raised before 385 — and places the basilica «circa 300 metri oltre il Colosseo», about 300 metres beyond the Colosseum.
places.history: The lower church was wrecked in the sack of 1084 by Robert Guiscard. The upper church was built in 1108 by Paschal II and restructured under Clement XI by Carlo Fontana, who made the Baroque facade and reused ancient granite columns in the arcaded portico. The bell tower is of the late seventeenth or early eighteenth century. The Mithraeum belongs to this site rather than standing as a separate one. The basilica is in Monti, and the neighbouring rione of Celio does not list it among its own monuments.

places.name: Basilica dei Santi Silvestro e Martino ai Monti
places.address: Viale del Monte Oppio 28, 00185 Roma RM
places.summary: A basilica whose title Roma Capitale traces to the fourth century, with a first church attributed to a third-century figure named Equizio.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the church and the adjoining convent were entrusted to the Carmelites by Boniface VIII, on condition that they set up a house of study there. The Comune's page gives two different years for that entrustment in two places, so no year is given here.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Pudenziana
places.summary: A church on via Urbana, in Monti.
places.history: turismoroma has no page for it and no source from the parish states more.

places.name: Basilica di Santo Stefano Rotondo al Celio
places.address: Via Santo Stefano Rotondo 7, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A basilica whose name says «al Celio» but which is in Monti. Via di Santo Stefano Rotondo is itself named as the line between the two rioni in both perimeter descriptions.
places.history: turismoroma returns no page for the church.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
places.summary: A Jesuit church on via del Quirinale. Its own website publishes its hours: Tuesday to Sunday 9.00–12.00 and 15.00–18.00, closed Monday.
places.history: The church fronts via del Quirinale, which Roma Capitale's perimeter description names as one of the rione's boundaries. This record makes no claim about the rione of piazza del Quirinale, which both neighbouring rioni's own descriptions call the line between them.

places.name: Chiesa di San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
places.summary: «San Carlino»: the church and convent the Spanish Trinitarians gave to Francesco Borromini.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Borromini worked on it from 1638 to 1642, took it up again later, and died in 1667 with the front still under construction; the concave-convex facade is his last work. The interior is oval, on a giant order of composite columns, and the statue of St Charles Borromeo is by Antonio Raggi. The Chiostro del Borromini belongs to this same complex rather than standing separately. No postcode is given here: the one OpenStreetMap carries for the building is not a valid Italian CAP.

places.name: Chiesa di San Francesco di Paola
places.address: Piazza di San Francesco di Paola, Roma RM
places.summary: A church on its own piazza. Above it stand the Loggia Borgia and the Arco della Suburra, per the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione.
places.history: The Palazzo Borgia survives in this record as the loggia above the church rather than as a separate entry. The salita dei Borgia, which climbs beside it, runs partly along what the same article says is believed to be the ancient Vicus sceleratus.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Lucia in Selci
places.summary: A diaconia attested from the fifth century, with its attached monastery, per the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione.
places.history: Via in Selci follows the line of the ancient Vicus Suburranus and takes its name from the ancient paving stones found during works there, per the same article.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Caterina a Magnanapoli
places.summary: A church on largo Magnanapoli whose monastery absorbed the Torre delle Milizie until after 1910.
places.history: The source for this record is Roma Capitale's page for the Torre delle Milizie, which records the absorption. No per-place page for the church itself was obtained.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Quirico e Giulitta
places.address: Via Tor de' Conti, Roma RM
places.summary: A church on via Tor de' Conti which houses the Museo tipologico internazionale del presepio «Angelo Stefanucci».
places.history: The museum keeps its own website.

places.name: Cattedrale dei Santi Sergio e Bacco degli Ucraini
places.summary: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic cathedral in Rome, which OpenStreetMap records under the name Santi Sergio e Bacco in Suburra.
places.history: No source beyond OpenStreetMap states more than the name and the denomination.

places.name: Palazzo delle Esposizioni
places.summary: An exhibition building on via Nazionale. Its own site states that «Il Palazzo fu inaugurato il 21 gennaio 1883» — the palace was inaugurated on 21 January 1883.
places.history: No source states more than the inauguration date and the address.

places.name: Palazzo del Viminale
places.summary: The seat of the Ministero dell'Interno, on piazza del Viminale, five storeys high.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the building was conceived by Giovanni Giolitti; that a ministerial decree of 1911 gave the design to Manfredo Manfredi; that the definitive project was approved on 15 October 1912 by the Ministero dei Lavori Pubblici at a total cost of 8 million, and confirmed on 23 October 1912 by the Consiglio di Stato; and that it was inaugurated on 9 July 1925.

places.name: Palazzo Pallavicini Rospigliosi
places.summary: A palace built for Cardinal Scipione Borghese in the early 1600s on the site of the Terme di Costantino.
places.history: Roma Capitale names Flaminio Ponzio and then Carlo Maderno as its architects, and the Fleming Giovanni Vasanzio for the garden and the nymphaeum. It passed later to the Altemps, the Bentivoglio and the Lante.

places.name: Palazzo Koch
places.summary: The head office of the Banca d'Italia, whose own site advertises «Visite a Palazzo Koch».
places.history: The Italian Wikipedia article on the rione dates the building to 1882 and gives the architect as Gaetano Koch. The head-office role and the visits come from the bank itself.

places.name: Palazzo Brancaccio
places.summary: A palace on via Merulana. The Italian Wikipedia article on the rione dates it 1886–1912 and names Luca Carimini as its architect.
places.history: The same article records the palace as the former seat of the Museo nazionale d'arte orientale Giuseppe Tucci, since moved to EUR. Two cautions about where it stands: the geocoded address returns the postcode 00185, which is the Esquilino code, on a building the boundary tests place in Monti; and via Merulana is a boundary street in Roma Capitale's own perimeter for the rione rather than an interior one.

places.name: Palazzo del Grillo
places.summary: A palace on piazza del Grillo which the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione dates to the seventeenth century.
places.history: Roma Capitale's page for the Torre del Grillo corroborates the family connection: the tower was bought by the del Grillo in 1675 and absorbed into the left wing of the palazzo. The century comes from Wikipedia; the purchase and the absorption come from Roma Capitale.

places.name: Villa Aldobrandini
places.summary: A hanging garden held inside retaining walls, entered from via Mazzarino by a steep stair.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Monsignor Giulio Vitelli bought a vineyard at Monte Magnanapoli in 1566 and that Carlo Lambardi restored the property; that it was sold to Clement VIII in 1600 and given the following year to his nephew Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini; and that Giacomo Della Porta added the stairs, the loggias and a continuous garden facade. The art collection had been left to the cardinal in 1598 by Lucrezia d'Este. The opening of via Nazionale after 1870 drastically cut the grounds.

places.name: Villa Sforza ai Quattro Cantoni
places.summary: A villa built between 1620 and 1634, per the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione.
places.history: The same article records the building as the Lazio and Abruzzo territorial directorate of the Agenzia delle Dogane e dei Monopoli.

places.name: Palazzo dell'ISTAT
places.summary: The seat of ISTAT, the Italian national statistics institute, which the institute's own contact pages confirm.
places.history: The Italian Wikipedia article on the rione dates the building to 1931.

places.name: Porta Asinaria
places.summary: A gate in the Aurelian wall that originally carried the Via Asinaria through a single arch between two square towers.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that it was monumentalised in the early fifth century under Honorius (395–423) with two semicircular towers and a travertine-faced arch, an inner counter-gate and a guard court, its towers raised to nearly double their height, to four storeys. Belisarius entered Rome by it in 536, Totila ten years later, and Henry IV during the sack.

places.name: Porta Metronia
places.summary: A plain single unornamented arch cut in the brick curtain of the Aurelian wall — a posterula of the third order which, Roma Capitale says, was never monumentalised as the Pinciana and the Asinaria were.
places.history: In 1122 Callixtus II routed the Acqua Mariana through it, and the gate was closed to people and to goods, becoming a fortified water gate. The neighbouring rione of Celio concedes the gate to Monti in its own article.

places.name: Museo storico della fisica e Centro studi e ricerche Enrico Fermi
places.summary: The CREF, in the building of the ragazzi di via Panisperna. The institution describes itself as having a double nature: research centre and historical museum.
places.history: Its own site gives two addresses, and both are correct because they are two doors of one building. The registered office and postal address is Via Panisperna 89a, 00184; the visitor entrance is at piazza del Viminale 1, 00184. That is why other records place the museum on piazza del Viminale while OpenStreetMap places it on via Panisperna.

places.name: Museo tipologico internazionale del presepio Angelo Stefanucci
places.address: Via Tor de' Conti, Roma RM
places.summary: A museum of nativity scenes inside the church of Santi Quirico e Giulitta, on via Tor de' Conti. It keeps its own website.
places.history: The record rests on the museum's own site and on the Italian Wikipedia article on the rione, which places the museum in the church.

places.name: Museo Vite di IMI
places.summary: A museum on via Labicana devoted to the Italian Military Internees. Its own site describes a historical and educational route through the «resistenza senza armi» — the unarmed resistance — of 1943 to 1945.
places.history: The site names the rooms of the route: 8 settembre; La cattura e il viaggio; Il campo: l'internamento; Il lavoro coatto; La liberazione e il rimpatrio; and Il Cortile della Memoria.

places.name: Pontificia Università San Tommaso d'Aquino (Angelicum)
places.summary: The university its own site calls the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas – Angelicum, on largo Angelicum. The church of Santi Domenico e Sisto belongs to the same complex.
places.history: No immunity, exemption or special legal status of any kind is claimed for it here. Beyond what its own site states, no further detail was obtained.

places.name: Pontificio Istituto Teologico Giovanni Paolo II
places.summary: An institute whose own site gives its full title as the Pontificio Istituto Teologico Giovanni Paolo II «per le Scienze del Matrimonio e della Famiglia – Sede Centrale».
places.history: No source states a street address or any further detail.

places.name: Via dei Fori Imperiali
places.summary: The road opened in 1932 as via dell'Impero. It is the boundary between Monti and Campitelli: the fora on the north side, Trajan's and Augustus's, are Monti's, and those on the south side are Campitelli's.
places.history: The Italian Wikipedia article on the rione records that the entire sixteenth-century quarter behind the road, centred on via Alessandrina, was demolished to make it, and that excavations from the late 1990s have brought back both imperial-age construction and the foundations of those demolished buildings.

places.name: Mercato Monti Urban Market
places.summary: A market at Via Leonina 46/48, in Monti. The address is from its own site.
places.history: No source establishes how long the market has traded.

places.name: Ai Tre Scalini
places.summary: A vineria on via Panisperna. Its own site gives the address twice and describes the place as being in «Rione Monti».
places.history: An American vine grows on the facade, per the same site. No source establishes how long the business has traded.

entries.name: Colonna Traiana
entries.note: Seventeen monolithic drums around an internal spiral stair of 185 steps, with Trajan's ashes in the base and a figure of St Peter put on top by Sixtus V in 1587.

entries.name: Mercati di Traiano — Museo dei Fori Imperiali
entries.note: Six levels of Roman building stepped up the Quirinal slope; the museum inside was inaugurated in the autumn of 2007, and the Torre delle Milizie is entered through it.

entries.name: Foro di Augusto
entries.note: Inaugurated in 2 BC around the temple of Mars Ultor, three of whose Carrara marble columns still stand, with a firewall of peperino and travertine up to thirty-three metres behind it.

entries.name: Via dei Fori Imperiali
entries.note: Opened in 1932 as via dell'Impero over a demolished sixteenth-century quarter, and the line that puts the fora of Trajan and Augustus on the Monti side and the rest in Campitelli.

entries.name: Torre delle Milizie
entries.note: About fifty metres of brick, attributed to the Conti di Segni at the start of the thirteenth century; a mid-fourteenth-century earthquake brought down the third storey and started the lean.

entries.name: Torre dei Conti
entries.note: Built around 1203 by Innocent III for his brother Riccardo and once about 60 metres high; its cellars incorporate a squared-tufa exedra of the Forum of Peace.

entries.name: Torre del Grillo
entries.note: Built in 1223 on Trajanic remains; the del Grillo bought it in 1675 and added the corner eagles and the inscription EX MARCHIONE DE GRILLIS, and Renato Guttuso later painted in it.

entries.name: Torre dei Capocci
entries.note: Thirty-six metres of brick taken from the Terme di Traiano, its colour changing at third-floor level where the surrounding houses were pulled down; not visitable inside.

entries.name: Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano
entries.note: Roma Capitale names it among the rione's monuments; under the Lateran Treaty of 1929 the Holy See owns it, but the ground is Italian and Italian law applies to visitors.

entries.name: Battistero lateranense
entries.note: An octagon on eight porphyry columns beside the basilica, with Borromini's external frieze of 1657 and a green basalt font under a bronze cover by Ciro Ferri.

entries.name: Palazzo del Laterano
entries.note: The Lateran Pacts were signed inside on 11 February 1929 and took their name from it; the Museo storico vaticano stands within, on Italian soil.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore
entries.note: Nave mosaics of the fifth century, the Sistina and Paolina chapels of Sixtus V and Paul V, and the snow miracle commemorated on 5 August.

entries.name: Basilica di San Clemente al Laterano
entries.note: Two churches stacked over Republican-era buildings and a Mithraeum: the lower wrecked in Robert Guiscard's sack of 1084, the upper built in 1108 by Paschal II.

entries.name: Chiesa di Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
entries.note: Publishes its hours on its own site: Tuesday to Sunday 9.00–12.00 and 15.00–18.00, closed Monday.

links.note: Via dei Fori Imperiali is the Monti/Campitelli boundary. The fora south of the road, and the ticketed walkway between them, belong to Campitelli.
Trastevere is rione XIII in Roma Capitale's toponymic list of Rome's 22 rioni; Monti is rione I.
Borgo is rione XIV in Roma Capitale's toponymic list of Rome's 22 rioni; Monti is rione I.
